into the IRMS as a gas (CO2 or H2) which is then ionized by electron impact under vacuum and accelerated from the source as
an ion beam (Fig. 3). The ionized gas sample is then accelerated through an evacuated ﬂight tube by an electrical gradient, during
which the ions of different mass are separated by a magnetic ﬁeld. The ion ﬂight for each gas species is then terminated on impact
with a faraday cup or collector. An array of these cups are conﬁgured to measure the current for each of the charged species of a gas
and the isotope ratio is then measured for each sample and then compared with a reference of known isotope abundance, typically
being either CO2 or H2.
Traditionally the introduction of the sample is through a dual-inlet system. This allows an unknown specimen to be measured
against a known reference pure gas and the isotope abundance expressed using the delta notation (di) and permil unit (0/00). The
delta permil value is essentially the relative difference of the isotopic ratios for each of the two gases. Originally introduced by
geochemists to express isotope abundances for natural samples collected from around the world, delta value in permil is calculated
as follows:
